recipe.history:
The true yam — Dioscorea species — is one of the oldest cultivated crops on earth, with archaeological evidence of its cultivation in West Africa dating back at least ten thousand years. It is a foundational food across a vast swath of the tropical and subtropical world: West Africa, the Caribbean, South and Southeast Asia, and Oceania, where it is grown not merely as sustenance but as a marker of status, wealth, and ceremonial importance. Among the Yoruba of Nigeria, yam festivals mark the agricultural calendar; the igba iri ji, or New Yam Festival, is one of the most significant cultural events of the year, celebrating the harvest with feasting, music, and ritual gratitude. True yams can reach extraordinary sizes — some varieties exceeding 150 pounds — and their starchy white or purple flesh is denser and less sweet than what Americans typically call yam, which is in fact a sweet potato, an unrelated species from the morning glory family that was given the name yam by African-American communities who recognized in it a distant echo of the nyami of their West African homelands.

The American sweet potato — routinely and defiantly called yam in home kitchens and on restaurant menus across the South — became embedded in American cooking through the agriculture of the colonial South, where it thrived in hot, humid conditions and became a staple of African-American foodways. By the twentieth century it was ubiquitous at holiday tables and soul food restaurants, appearing in casseroles, pies, and savory preparations. Its culinary migration into burger culture came through the sweet-savory trend of the 2000s and 2010s, when chefs began exploring sweetness as a counterpoint to the savory intensity of beef. Yam purée — smooth, slightly sweet, warmly spiced — became an unexpected but effective burger sauce, its starchy creaminess acting almost like a mayonnaise while contributing its own distinct character. Crispy yam chips added textural contrast, their caramelized edges providing crunch and a deeper, slightly charred sweetness against the soft interior of the purée.

I first put yam on a burger by accident, if I am being honest. I had leftover roasted sweet potato from Thanksgiving and a patty that needed something, and I found myself mashing the potato with a little butter and smoked paprika and spreading it on the bottom bun the way I would have spread mustard or mayo. The result stopped me mid-bite. There was something fundamentally correct about the combination — the sweetness of the potato pulling the savory umami of the beef into sharper relief, the starchy smoothness providing exactly the lubrication that a good sauce provides while tasting completely unlike any sauce I had used before. The crispy chips came later, when I needed textural contrast, and I understood that the burger had been waiting for both things at once: the yielding purée below and the brittle crunch on top, the soft and the crisp, the simple and the composed.

Medium rare is the internal temperature at which a burger patty most closely resembles the best version of itself — the version the animal was working toward. At 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, the sugars in the yam purée beneath the patty and the natural sweetness of the beef fat above it are in conversation with each other, neither one cooked past the point of nuance. A well-done patty has lost the capacity for this kind of conversation; it has only one register, and that register is grey and resigned. The yam purée in this burger is sweet and warm and generous; it deserves a patty that is equally generous, equally alive to the moment. Cook it to medium rare. Rest it properly. Let it speak.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
1 medium sweet potato, peeled and sliced paper-thin on a mandoline (about 1/16 inch)
neutral oil for frying (vegetable or canola)
1/2 small red onion, very thinly sliced
instructions: 1. Roast the yams for purée: Preheat oven to 400°F (205°C). Pierce sweet potatoes all over with a fork and place on a foil-lined baking sheet. Roast 50–60 minutes until completely tender when pierced with a knife and caramelized juices begin to bubble from the skin. Let cool slightly, then split and scoop the flesh into a bowl.

2. Make the purée: Mash the sweet potato flesh with butter, crème fraîche, smoked paprika, cinnamon, nutmeg, cayenne, brown sugar, and salt until smooth and silky. Taste and adjust seasoning. Keep warm, or reheat gently before serving.

3. Make the bun dough: Combine warm milk, yeast, and sugar in the bowl of a stand mixer and let sit 5 minutes until foamy. Add flour, salt, butter, and egg and mix on medium with the dough hook for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic.
4. Transfer dough to a lightly oiled bowl, cover, and let rise until doubled, about 1 to 1.5 hours.
5. Divide dough into 4 equal portions. Shape each into a smooth ball, place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, cover, and let rise again until doubled and puffy, about 45 minutes.
6. Brush buns with egg wash and bake at 375°F (190°C) for 16–18 minutes until deep golden. Cool on a wire rack.

7. Fry the yam chips: Heat 2 inches of neutral oil in a heavy-bottomed saucepan to 325°F (165°C). Working in small batches, fry the sweet potato slices for 3–4 minutes, stirring gently, until golden and crisp. Transfer to a paper towel-lined tray with a slotted spoon. Immediately toss with smoked paprika, cayenne, and salt. The chips will crisp further as they cool.

8. Prepare the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions of about 170g each. Form gently into patties about 3/4 inch thick with a thumb dimple in the center. Season both sides with salt, pepper, and smoked paprika. Refrigerate 15 minutes.
9. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook patties 3 minutes first side without pressing. Flip and cook 2–3 minutes second side.
10. Lay a slice of pepper jack on each patty. Add a splash of water, cover immediately, and steam 30–45 seconds until cheese is melted.
11. Transfer patties to a resting rack and rest 3–4 minutes. Target internal temperature is 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare.
12. Toss spinach with olive oil and a pinch of salt.
13. Split and toast buns cut-side down in a dry skillet over medium heat until golden, about 1–2 minutes.

14. Assemble: Spread a generous layer of warm yam purée on the bottom bun. Place the cheesed patty on top. Add the thinly sliced red onion. Layer on a handful of dressed spinach. Top with a generous pile of crispy yam chips. Finish with flaky sea salt. Set the top bun in place and serve immediately.
